bamo-bamo8-2026-a.title: Work on the triangular grid
bamo-bamo8-2026-a.body:
Put the trapezoid on coordinates: $A=(0,0)$, $B=(2,0)$, $C=\left(\tfrac32,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$, $D=\left(\tfrac12,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$. Then $AB=2$ and $BC=CD=DA=1$, and the angles at $A$ and $B$ are $60^\circ$. In fact $\mathcal{T}$ is made of three unit equilateral triangles, so it is natural to draw everything on a grid of equilateral triangles. A trapezoid similar to $\mathcal{T}$ at scale $s$ has sides $s, s, s, 2s$ and angles $60^\circ, 60^\circ, 120^\circ, 120^\circ$.

**(a) Four pieces at scale $\tfrac12$.** Let $\ell$ be the midline $y=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}$; it meets $AD$ at $M=\left(\tfrac14,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\right)$ and $BC$ at $N=\left(\tfrac74,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\right)$. On $\ell$ mark $E=\left(\tfrac34,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\right)$ and $F=\left(\tfrac54,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\right)$, which are $\tfrac12$ apart and symmetric about the axis $x=1$. On $AB$ mark $P=\left(\tfrac12,0\right)$ and $Q=\left(\tfrac32,0\right)$. Draw the segments $EF$, $DE$, $CF$, $PE$, $QF$. The four pieces are:

- $DCFE$ (upside down): $DC=1$, $EF=\tfrac12$, $DE=CF=\tfrac12$.
- $PQFE$ (its mirror image in $\ell$): $PQ=1$, $EF=\tfrac12$, $PE=QF=\tfrac12$.
- $APED$ (tilted): $AD=1$ is parallel to $PE$, which has length $\tfrac12$, and $AP=ED=\tfrac12$.
- $QBCF$ (the mirror image of $APED$ in the line $x=1$): $BC=1$, $QF=\tfrac12$, $QB=FC=\tfrac12$.

Each piece has sides $\tfrac12,\tfrac12,\tfrac12,1$, with the side of length $1$ parallel to the opposite side, so each is congruent to $\mathcal{T}$ scaled by $\tfrac12$. The pieces fill $\mathcal{T}$ without overlap.

**(b) Nine pieces at scale $\tfrac13$.** Let $E=(1,0)$ be the midpoint of $AB$ and draw $ED$ and $EC$. This cuts $\mathcal{T}$ into three unit equilateral triangles $ADE$, $DCE$, $ECB$.

Now cut one unit equilateral triangle, say $ADE$ with center $O=\left(\tfrac12,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{6}\right)$, into three pieces. Mark the points one third of the way along each side, going around the triangle: $A_1$ on $AD$ with $AA_1=\tfrac13$, $D_1$ on $DE$ with $DD_1=\tfrac13$, and $E_1$ on $EA$ with $EE_1=\tfrac13$. Join each of $A_1$, $D_1$, $E_1$ to $O$. The segment $A_1O$ is horizontal (parallel to $AE$) and has length $\tfrac13$, and the same holds for the other two segments after rotating by $120^\circ$. The piece $AA_1OE_1$ has $AE_1=\tfrac23$ parallel to $A_1O=\tfrac13$, and $AA_1=OE_1=\tfrac13$. So it is $\mathcal{T}$ scaled by $\tfrac13$, and the other two pieces $A_1DD_1O$ and $E_1OD_1E$ are its rotations by $\pm120^\circ$ about $O$.

Do the same in each of the three triangles. This gives nine congruent trapezoids, each similar to $\mathcal{T}$ at scale $\tfrac13$. (This dissection is not the only one.) ∎

bamo-bamo8-2026-b.title: Monotonicity, then pin down b and c
bamo-bamo8-2026-b.body:
If $a<1$ then $b=0$ and $c=0$, so $ac=0\ne 42$. So $a\ge 1$.

**At most one solution.** If $a$ increases, then $b=\lfloor a\rfloor$ cannot decrease, so $ab$ increases and $c=\lfloor ab\rfloor$ cannot decrease. Hence $ac$ strictly increases with $a$ (because $c\ge 1$ for $a\ge 1$). So $ac=42$ has at most one solution.

**Bracketing.** For an integer $a$ we get $b=a$, $c=a^2$, so $ac=a^3$. Since $3^3=27<42<64=4^3$, the solution must satisfy $3<a<4$. Then $b=3$ and $9<3a<12$, so $c\in\{9,10,11\}$. Since $a=\dfrac{42}{c}<4$, we need $c>10.5$, so $c=11$ and $a=\dfrac{42}{11}$.

**Check.** With $a=\tfrac{42}{11}\approx 3.82$: $b=3$, $ab=\tfrac{126}{11}=11\tfrac{5}{11}$, $c=11$, and $ac=42$. ✓

**Answer: $a=\dfrac{42}{11}$, and this is the only value.**

bamo-bamo8-2026-b.title: Case on b directly
bamo-bamo8-2026-b.body:
As before $a\ge1$, so write $b=n\ge1$. Then $n\le a<n+1$, so $n^2\le ab<n^2+n$ and therefore $n^2\le c\le n^2+n-1$. This gives $42=ac\ge n\cdot n^2=n^3$, so $n\le 3$, and $42=ac<(n+1)(n^2+n)=n(n+1)^2$, so $n(n+1)^2>42$, which forces $n\ge 3$ ($2\cdot 9=18$). So $n=3$, $c\in\{9,10,11\}$, and $a=42/c$ has to lie in $[3,4)$. The candidates are $42/9\approx4.67$, $42/10=4.2$, and $42/11\approx3.82$, so only $c=11$ works. Checking $a=\tfrac{42}{11}$ shows that $c$ really is $11$.

**Answer: $a=\dfrac{42}{11}$**

bamo-bamo8-2026-c.title: Which edge is halved, then compare edges
bamo-bamo8-2026-c.body:
Let $B$ have edges $\ell\ge w\ge h$.

**The cut.** Each piece is a box, and the cut face is one face of each piece. The face of a piece opposite its cut face is not the cut, so it lies in a face of $B$. Hence the cut plane is parallel to a pair of opposite faces of $B$. Each piece keeps the two edges of $B$ that run parallel to the cut, and the remaining edge of $B$ is split into two parts. For the pieces to be congruent, the two parts must be equal, so the cut halves one edge of $B$.

**It must halve the longest edge.** Each piece has half the volume of $B$, so it is $B$ scaled by some factor $\tfrac1r$ with $r>1$, and all its edges are shorter than the corresponding edges of $B$. In particular its longest edge is $\tfrac{\ell}{r}<\ell$. If we halved $w$ or $h$, each piece would still have an edge of length $\ell$, which is impossible. So the pieces are $w\times h\times\tfrac{\ell}{2}$.

**Matching the edges.** The shortest edge of a piece must be $\tfrac hr<h$, so $\tfrac{\ell}{2}<h$. Thus the edges of a piece, from longest to shortest, are $w\ge h>\tfrac{\ell}{2}$, and they must equal $\tfrac{\ell}{r},\tfrac{w}{r},\tfrac{h}{r}$:
$$\ell=rw,\qquad w=rh,\qquad h=\frac{r\ell}{2}.$$
Multiplying the three equations gives $\ell wh=\tfrac{r^3}{2}\,\ell wh$, so $r^3=2$ and $r=\sqrt[3]{2}$. (This also follows from the volume: each piece has volume $\tfrac12$ of $B$, so $\tfrac1{r^3}=\tfrac12$.)

**Construction.** Take $h=1$, $w=\sqrt[3]{2}$, $\ell=\sqrt[3]{4}$. Halving the longest edge gives pieces $\sqrt[3]{2}\times 1\times\tfrac{\sqrt[3]{4}}{2}$. Since $\tfrac{\sqrt[3]4}{2}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt[3]2}$, these edges are exactly $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt[3]2}\left(\sqrt[3]4,\ \sqrt[3]2,\ 1\right)$, so the pieces are similar to $B$. Any brick $\sqrt[3]{4}\,t\times\sqrt[3]{2}\,t\times t$ works, and these are the only ones. (This is the idea behind the A-series paper sizes, whose sides are in ratio $\sqrt2$; here a box needs ratio $\sqrt[3]2$.)

**Answer: e.g. $\sqrt[3]{4}\times\sqrt[3]{2}\times1$.** ∎

bamo-bamo8-2026-d.title: Use a + b + c = 4 and Pythagoras
bamo-bamo8-2026-d.body:
**All eight triangles are congruent.** The figure does not change under a $90^\circ$ rotation about the common center (each square maps to itself). It also does not change under the reflection in the line through the center and a crossing point of the two squares, which swaps the two squares. Using these symmetries, any one of the eight triangles can be moved onto any other.

**Each side has length $a+b+c$.** Look at one side of a square. The other square cuts it into three segments: the end pieces are legs of two of the small triangles, and the middle piece is a side of the octagon, which is the hypotenuse of the triangle that sticks out beyond this side. The $90^\circ$ rotation carries the corner triangle at one end of this side to the corner triangle at the other end, and it turns the leg on this side into the leg on the neighbouring side. So the two end pieces are the two *different* legs of congruent triangles, of lengths $a$ and $b$, and the side has length $a+c+b=4$.

**Finish.** Using $a+b+c=4$ and $a^2+b^2=c^2$:
$$4(a+b-c)=(a+b+c)(a+b-c)=(a+b)^2-c^2=a^2+2ab+b^2-c^2=2ab.$$
So $a+b-c=\tfrac12ab$, which is the area of the right triangle. ∎

bamo-bamo8-2026-d.title: Compute the octagon's area
bamo-bamo8-2026-d.body:
As in the first approach, the eight triangles are congruent and $a+b+c=4$. All eight sides of the octagon have length $c$, and each side lies on a side of one of the squares, at distance $2$ from the center. Joining the center to the eight vertices splits the octagon into eight triangles with base $c$ and height $2$, so the octagon has area $8\cdot\tfrac12\cdot c\cdot 2=8c$.

One square (area $16$) consists of the octagon and four of the small triangles. So each small triangle has area
$$\frac{16-8c}{4}=4-2c=(a+b+c)-2c=a+b-c.$$ ∎

bamo-bamo8-2026-e.title: Yes means same team, No means different team
bamo-bamo8-2026-e.body:
Suppose person $P$ is asked about the person $Q$ on their left:

| $P$ | $Q$ | $P$ answers |
|---|---|---|
| Truth-Teller | Truth-Teller | Yes |
| Truth-Teller | Liar | No |
| Liar | Truth-Teller | No |
| Liar | Liar | Yes |

So "Yes" means exactly that $P$ and $Q$ have the **same** role, and "No" means they have **different** roles. This is true for Lou too, whatever her role is.

Walk once around the circle, from each person to the person on their left. Every "No" marks a switch between the two roles. Since we come back to the starting person, we must switch an even number of times. So when everyone (Lou included) has answered, the total number of "No" answers must be even.

The other six students gave three "No"s. So the correct answer from Lou, whatever her role, is a fourth "No". (Answering "Yes" would leave an odd number of "No"s, which is impossible for correct answers.)

**Answer: Lou should say "No".**

bamo-bamo12-2026-4.title: Invariant mod 16, then an inductive construction
bamo-bamo12-2026-4.body:
We prove: **Fran can write $a^2$ if and only if $a\not\equiv 2 \pmod 4$.** Since $2026\equiv 2\pmod 4$, she cannot write $2026^2$. But $2026^{2026}=\left(2026^{1013}\right)^2$ and $4\mid 2026^{1013}$, so she can write $2026^{2026}$.

**Facts about squares mod 16.** Every square is $\equiv 0,1,4,9\pmod{16}$ (check $a=0,1,\dots,7$; $a$ and $-a$, and $a$ and $a+8$, have the same square mod $16$). Also $a^2\equiv 4\pmod{16}$ exactly when $a\equiv 2\pmod 4$. If $a=4m+2$, then $a^2=16(m^2+m)+4$. Conversely, if $a^2\equiv4$, then $a=2m$ is even and $4m^2\equiv 4\pmod{16}$, so $m^2\equiv1\pmod4$ and $m$ is odd.

**Part 1: $a^2$ with $a\equiv 2\pmod 4$ never appears.** We show that the following two statements stay true throughout:

- (I) every number on the board is $\equiv 0,1,2,9$ or $10\pmod{16}$;
- (II) every perfect square on the board is $\equiv 0,1$ or $9\pmod{16}$.

At the start the board has only $2026\equiv 10\pmod{16}$, which is not a square ($45^2=2025$). Suppose (I) and (II) hold, and Fran makes a move.

- *Splitting* $N=a^2+b^2$ into $a^2,b^2$. If $a^2\equiv4$, then $N\equiv 4+\{0,1,4,9\}=\{4,5,8,13\}\pmod{16}$, which contradicts (I) for $N$. So each new number is a square $\equiv0,1,9$, and (I), (II) still hold.
- *Joining* $a^2,b^2$ into $a^2+b^2$. By (II), $a^2,b^2\in\{0,1,9\}\pmod{16}$, so the sum lies in $\{0,1,2,9,10\}$ (note $9+9=18\equiv2$). This keeps (I), and if the sum is a square, it is not $\equiv4$, which keeps (II).

So $a^2\equiv 4\pmod{16}$ never appears. In particular, no $a^2$ with $a\equiv2\pmod4$ appears.

**Part 2: every other square appears.** A useful combined move: if $a^2$ and $b^2$ are on the board and $a^2+b^2=c^2+d^2$ with $c\ne d$, Fran can write $a^2+b^2$ and then split it into $c^2$ and $d^2$. Write this as $(a,b)\to(c,d)$.

*Opening.* $2026=45^2+1^2$ gives $45^2$ and $1^2$. Then $45^2=2025=36^2+27^2$ gives $36^2$ and $27^2$. Next:
- $(1,27)\to(17,21)$ since $730=1+729=289+441$;
- $(1,17)\to(11,13)$ since $290=121+169$;
- $13^2=169=5^2+12^2$ (split), giving $5^2,12^2$;
- $(1,12)\to(8,9)$ since $145=64+81$;
- $(1,8)\to(4,7)$ since $65=16+49$;
- $(7,9)\to(3,11)$ since $130=9+121$.

Now the board has $a^2$ for every $a\le 13$ with $a\not\equiv 2\pmod 4$, namely $a=1,3,4,5,7,8,9,11,12,13$.

*Induction.* For $k\ge 4$ we use the identities (each side minus the other is a difference of squares):
$$(4k-3)^2+(2k+1)^2=(4k-1)^2+(2k-3)^2,$$
$$(4k-4)^2+(2k+3)^2=(4k)^2+(2k-5)^2,$$
$$(4k-5)^2+(2k+5)^2=(4k+1)^2+(2k-7)^2.$$
For example, the first one holds because $(4k-1)^2-(4k-3)^2=2(8k-4)=16k-8$ and $(2k+1)^2-(2k-3)^2=4(4k-2)=16k-8$. The other two check the same way.

Assume all $a^2$ with $a\le 4k-3$ and $a\not\equiv2\pmod4$ are on the board (true for $k=4$). For $k\ge4$, the numbers $4k-3,4k-4,4k-5,2k+1,2k+3,2k+5$ are all at most $4k-3$. None of them is $\equiv2\pmod 4$: three are odd, and $4k-4\equiv 0$. In each identity the two numbers on the left are distinct, and so are the two on the right, and they are positive ($2k-7\ge1$). So the three moves
$$(4k-3,\,2k+1)\to(4k-1,\,2k-3),\quad (4k-4,\,2k+3)\to(4k,\,2k-5),\quad (4k-5,\,2k+5)\to(4k+1,\,2k-7)$$
are legal, and they produce $(4k-1)^2,(4k)^2,(4k+1)^2$. Now every $a\le 4(k+1)-3$ with $a\not\equiv2\pmod 4$ is covered, because $4k+2$ is the only number skipped. By induction, every $a^2$ with $a\not\equiv 2\pmod 4$ can be written.

**Answer: $2026^2$ — no; $2026^{2026}$ — yes.** ∎

bamo-bamo12-2026-5.title: Add a card 0 and read the deck on a circle
bamo-bamo12-2026-5.body:
**A circular model.** Add an imaginary card $0$ and place the cards $0,d_1,d_2,\dots,d_N$ clockwise on a circle, where $d_1,\dots,d_N$ is the deck from top to bottom. Reading clockwise starting just after $0$ recovers the deck. Two circles count as the same if one is a rotation of the other; only the cyclic order matters.

**One step = swapping the labels $0$ and $k$.** Suppose the deck is $X,k,Y$ ($X$ the cards above $k$, $Y$ those below, either possibly empty). The step produces $Y,k,X$. On the circle the cyclic order before the step is $(0,X,k,Y)$ and after it is $(0,Y,k,X)$. If instead we keep the circle and simply exchange the labels $0$ and $k$, we get $(k,X,0,Y)$. Read starting from $0$, that is $(0,Y,k,X)$, the same cyclic order. So each step is just "exchange the labels $0$ and $k$ on the circle".

**One grand swap = add $1$ to every label.** A grand swap exchanges the labels $0\leftrightarrow1$, then $0\leftrightarrow2$, …, then $0\leftrightarrow N$, in that order. Follow one spot on the circle:
- If it holds $0$, step $1$ makes it $1$, and later steps (which involve $0$ and $k\ge2$) do not touch it. So $0\mapsto 1$.
- If it holds $j$ with $1\le j\le N-1$: steps $1,\dots,j-1$ do not touch it, step $j$ makes it $0$, step $j+1$ makes it $j+1$, and steps $j+2,\dots,N$ do not touch it. So $j\mapsto j+1$.
- If it holds $N$, only step $N$ touches it, making it $0$. So $N\mapsto 0$.

So a grand swap replaces every label $j$ by $j+1 \pmod{N+1}$, without moving the spots.

**Conclusion.** After $N+1$ grand swaps, every spot has its original label again. So the circle is exactly the original one, and reading it clockwise after $0$ gives the original deck. ∎

(Check with the example: the circle $(0,1,2,4,3)$ becomes $(1,2,3,0,4)$, i.e. the deck $4,1,2,3$, as computed in the problem.)
